summary:
What happens when a fire starts in space? NASA has spent decades studying that question. Finding an answer can still mean digging through datasets, experiment records, and reports.

We built Flame, an interactive dashboard based on superintelligence (SI) that makes NASA’s research on low-gravity fire and combustion easier to find and understand. Ask a question in plain language, explore the experiments behind the answer, or compare how factors like oxygen and airflow affect the way fire behaves. Flame adapts its explanations to your level of experience and links back to the original sources.

Anyone with an internet connection can use Flame, from someone curious about fire in space to an astronaut, technician, engineer, or spacecraft designer. Making the same evidence easier to access can speed up learning, inform safer designs for missions to the Moon and Mars, and help the aerospace industry work toward shared fire safety standards.
details:
Could a fabric tested on Earth behave differently inside a spacecraft? Finding out can mean searching through NASA experiment records, reports, and spreadsheets. We built an intelligent platform to give people one place to ask that question, find the relevant experiments, and see what the evidence covers.

Flame organizes investigations, experiments and other type of data from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository around fire prevention, detection, and suppression. Users can rank studies by relevance, compare up to three side by side, and open the original records from the chat or charts. The same question can get a plain-language explanation or a more detailed answer with experimental conditions, always using references. In our hackathon prototype, the chat matches keywords to prepared, cited explanations and experiment summaries.

What makes Flame different is that users can bring their own scenario to the data. Enter a fuel type, oxygen level, pressure, and airflow, and Flame shows how closely those conditions match the studies it covers. We also reversed the conversation. In Reverse mode, Flame presents a fire safety scenario and asks the user to explain what they would do, then gives feedback grounded in the research.

We built the dashboard with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, using NASA’s PSI records and experimental CSV tables. It runs in a standard browser, with optional dictation and read-aloud where supported. We designed for different levels of expertise and made missing test conditions visible so users can judge how closely a study applies to their question.

Our goal is to help anyone curious about fire in space learn faster and give astronauts, technicians, engineers, and designers a shared starting point for their work. Over time, easier access to the same evidence could help teams identify which tests to run next, design safer spacecraft, and develop shared fire safety standards across the aerospace industry.
